tagline.text: A half-day escape from Manila to a Batangas beach with floating bamboo raft cottages

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~3,000 (per person for a day trip, covering transport, entrance, and a shared cottage)

children.text: Matabungkay Beach is a beach several kilometers long in Lian, Batangas, a traditional getaway dating back to the 1950s and only 2–3 hours from Manila by road. Resorts line the shore, and the floating bamboo raft cottages are its trademark. It is a day-trip beach you choose for its closeness and ease rather than glamour.
Matabungkay is a beach village in the municipality of Lian at the western end of Batangas province. It lies about

from Manila (sources differ), which makes it an easy weekend trip. According to Wikipedia, Manila residents began coming here for weekends and day trips in the early 1950s, and the area became well known in the 1960s when wealthy families built beach houses along the shore. For a long time it was the go-to beach for family and company outings and group trips.

The beach runs along a long stretch of coast. The sand is fine and light gray to cream, looking white in strong sunlight. Resorts, shops, and houses stand side by side along the shoreline, so it is far from a quiet deserted-island scene, and many visitors describe it as a commercialized beach. In return, the water is clear and generally calm, which makes swimming easy for both children and adults, and the pricier resorts at either end of the beach make those ends quieter than the middle.

The symbol of this place is the floating bamboo raft cottage. A raft with a roof and a deck is moored in the sea a short way off the beach, and you eat, relax, and jump into the water from it. On May 18, 2002, the first Balsa Festival was held here to revive local tourism, hosted by Matabungkay Beach Resort & Hotel, with a raft race and a beachside concert. The festival schedule changes from year to year, so check before you go.
Corals and small fish are reported to be visible about

from shore, so it is a good place for easy snorkeling, and for better spots you rent a boat. Coral condition and water quality can change on crowded weekends, so do not set your expectations too high. It is more accurate to think of it as a nearby sea that Manila residents visit casually than as a glamorous resort destination like Angeles or Boracay. The thing that confuses first-time visitors most is how "entrance fees" relate to resorts. The beach itself is public and is said to be free to enter, but most of the beach adjoins resort grounds, so in practice you often go in through a resort. In that case the resort may charge about
per person, and some sources mention a day-tour entrance fee of about
depending on the season. Every resort handles this differently, so ask when you arrive and decide then. The environmental fee is reported at about
A cottage built from a roofed deck on a floating bamboo raft. Prices depend on size and group, but about
is the usual quote, and you can eat on the raft and jump straight into the sea, which makes it this beach's signature experience.
The beach faces the western sea, so the sky turns red around dusk. It helps to ask a local operator in advance about watching the sunset from a raft.
Along the shore there are secluded little coves like small sand pockets, and Matabungkay Beach Hotel is reported to offer a boat for cove hopping (about
per hour for up to 7 people). Rates can change, so confirm with the resort.
Corals and small fish are said to be visible about
from the water's edge. Some resorts rent snorkel gear for about
per hour. Do not step on the corals, and do not leave trash behind.
Resorts rent jet skis, banana boats, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, and pedal boats by the hour. Prices differ by resort, with quotes ranging from
per hour for kayaks, paddleboards, and pedal boats to about
per hour for a jet ski.

If you leave Manila at dawn, you can spend a full day here and return in the evening. The beach is public, so there is no entrance fee, and you pay only if you enter through a resort. Many people bring their own food.

blocks.title: Simple shops and market in Lian

children.text: Behind the beach there are shops and a small market where you can buy water, snacks, and souvenirs. Because this is a commercial strip, some visitors report touts and karaoke noise, so choose a resort at the end of the beach if you want a quieter feel.

items.title: One-day course
items.subtitle: A day at the sea starting at dawn

children.text: Take a van or bus bound for Lian or Calatagan from EDSA-Taft or the Pasay Rotonda area in Manila.
Get off at the junction to Matabungkay Beach and take a tricycle to the beach. On arrival, check the resort entrance fee and the environmental fee.
Claim a cottage or raft, unpack, and swim and snorkel. It is most comfortable before the sun gets high.
Have lunch at your cottage. Bring your own food or use the resort restaurant.
Try water sports such as kayaking or paddleboarding, or take a cove-hopping trip.
Watch the sunset, rinse off, and head out to the junction to catch a bus or van back.
Return transport thins out later in the day, so leave yourself time to move right after the sun goes down.

items.title: Two days, one night
items.subtitle: A relaxed stay at a resort

children.text: Leave Manila, check in at your resort, and enjoy the pool and the beach.
Watch the sunset from a raft and have dinner.
Get up early to walk the quiet beach and snorkel.
After checkout, continue on to Calatagan or Nasugbu, or head back to Manila.

Another route is to take a DLTB or BSC bus to Nasugbu and then switch to a jeepney at the Lian terminal (Nasugbu fare about

Bus and van fares and departure points change often. The fares above come from 2018 blog posts, so check current information before you leave.
Take SLEX and exit at Santa Rosa or Silang, head toward Tagaytay, continue toward Nasugbu, and follow the signs to Lian. It usually takes
2–3 hours

The most reliable beach weather is the dry season,
November–April
. The sun is strong and the water is clear, which is good for snorkeling. During Holy Week and long weekends the resorts fill up and the beach gets very crowded.
May
and
October
are relatively quiet but can bring showers, and during the

rainy season waves and weather change often, so beach plans are easily upset. Weekends are busy at any time of year, so choose a weekday if you want some space.

Along the beach there are several long-established resorts, such as Matabungkay Beach Resort & Hotel, Coral Beach Club, Bella Beach Resort, and White Castle Hotel and Resort. Accommodation ranges from budget to high-end, and rooms fill up quickly on weekends and holidays. Room rates vary widely by season, so check on a booking site. Each resort has its own pool, restaurant, cottages, and water-sports rental desk, so the atmosphere and prices differ a lot even on the same beach. Families will do well at a larger resort with a pool and restaurant, while those who want quiet rest suit the smaller resorts at the ends of the beach.

You can bring your own food, or eat at a resort restaurant or the shops behind the beach. Buying fresh seafood and asking your resort to cook it is also common, but whether this is allowed and what the cooking fee is depend on the resort. Because the beach is commercial, there can be noise and touts, so if rest is your goal, choose a quiet resort at one of the ends. The market behind the beach sells fruit, snacks, and bottled water cheaply, which is easier on the budget than resort mini-stores. Cottages are busiest after lunch, so it is better to claim yours early.
For a day trip, leave at dawn to get a long day and an easier trip home. Buses from Manila are said to run from early morning, but check the last departure time locally.
Entrance policy differs if you book a cottage through a resort, so check before you arrive.
The sand gets very hot around noon. Bring aqua shoes or sandals.
Use reef-friendly sunscreen and protect yourself from the sun with a hat or scarf.
Ask ahead about raft cottages and sunset rides so it is easier to secure a spot.
Bring an extra camera battery or a power bank, and a waterproof pouch.
Book accommodation ahead for weekends and holidays, and go on a weekday if you want quiet.
Take your trash with you. The environmental fee is collected to help protect the beach.
For water sports and snorkeling, always wear a life jacket, do not step on corals, and watch for currents and boat lanes.
Some tricycle drivers quote tourists high fares, so agree on the price before you get in.
The beach is commercialized, so there may be touts and karaoke noise.
Most fare and schedule information comes from 2018–2020 sources, so check current information locally.
In the rainy and typhoon seasons the waves and wind get rough, so check the weather and stay out of the water if conditions are bad.
Leave belongings in your cottage and take valuables with you when you step away.
Calatagan
is a nearby coastal area that continues on from Lian, with the stilts and beach resorts. One guide says jeepneys run to Calatagan from the Lian terminal, so check the route locally.
Masasa Beach
is another beach destination on the same Batangas coast.
Mount Batulao
on the Nasugbu side is easy to pair with the beach as a light trek.
On the way back to Manila you can stop at
Tagaytay
for the views and a meal.
